notes: The original Switch console (HAC-001) as torn down by iFixit; the 2019 HAC-001(-01) revision is named only in iFixit's battery listing, so its internals are unchecked. The console battery is glued down, and the Joy-Con controllers hold the rumble actuators, batteries and IR camera parts.

gaps: NVIDIA ODNX02-A2 is called 'presumably the Tegra X1-based SoC' by iFixit; the spec keeps that hedge.
The teardown is of the HAC-001 (step 4 names the model); the HAC-001(-01) internals are not checked.
An FCC ID seen only in search snippets is not used; fccid.io and fcc.report returned HTTP 403 to the researcher.

Left out: the European AC adapter HAC-002(EUR). It is not inside the console, Nintendo's information sheet does not say it is the boxed adapter, and the teardown unit's region is not stated. No North American adapter rating was found.
iFixit calls the HD Rumble motor a linear resonant actuator (LRA); it is filed under motor_dc_small, the nearest part type.

iFixit opened one HD Rumble actuator (step 21) and found a pair of 'powerful magnets'; magnet material is not called neodymium. The magnet qty of 4 assumes both Joy-Cons match (step 17 says each has an HD Rumble motor).
Named in the guide but not listed: MAX77620 PMIC, MAX17050 fuel gauge, BQ24193 charger (iFixit says possibly), Realtek ALC5639 codec, LSM6DS3H (iFixit says likely), Joy-Con STM32P411 controller.
Datasheet: only the Macronix MX25U4033E, which the guide links in step 20. None found for the console chips (MAX77620, MAX77621, K4F6E304HB, THGBMHG8C2LBAIL, BCM4356, ODNX02-A2).
Years come from iFixit's battery listing (2017 HAC-001, 2019 HAC-001(-01)); they are listing years, not launch dates.
method: iFixit Nintendo Switch Teardown (guide 78263): PDF export (25 pages) read with tools/research.js pdf, plus the API text; step 4 gives model HAC-001.
iFixit Nintendo Switch Console Battery listing: Battery Model HAC-003, 3.7 V, 4310 mAh, 16 Wh; compatibility lists HAC-001 (2017), HAC-001(-01) (2019) and the OLED HEG-001 (2021).
Macronix MX25U4033E datasheet (rev 1.9, 1.8V 4M-bit), opened as a PDF; the guide links it in step 20.
LCSC listing C2802896 (MX25U4033EZUI-12G) opens, but its datasheet PDF link returns an HTML page, so it is not cited.
Nintendo's European AC adapter information sheet (HAC-002(EUR)) was read and not used.
Refused to the researcher: fccid.io and fcc.report (HTTP 403).

comps.spec: HAC-003 lithium-ion battery, 3.7 V, 4310 mAh, 16 Wh, in the console
Metal plate that doubles as a heat sink, channelling heat from the heat pipe to the rear case (step 6); the heat pipe is held by Phillips screws (step 8)
Delta Electronics fan rated 5 V and 0.33 A, held by three screws with rubber vibration-damping mounts, under the I/O board (steps 8 and 9)
Maxim MAX77621AEWI+T three-phase buck regulator, two on the board (step 11)
NVIDIA ODNX02-A2, which iFixit says is presumably the Tegra X1-based SoC (step 11)
Samsung K4F6E304HB-MGCH 2 GB LPDDR4 DRAM, two chips for 4 GB in total (step 11)
Toshiba THGBMHG8C2LBAIL 32 GB eMMC NAND flash on its own removable PCB (step 10)
Broadcom/Cypress BCM4356 802.11ac 2x2 Wi-Fi with Bluetooth 4.1 SoC (step 11)
6.2-inch multi-touch LCD, 1280 x 720; the LCD is removable and the digitizer is a separate part (steps 1, 14 and 15)
Stereo speakers lightly adhered to the rear case (steps 1 and 13)
HD Rumble motor, which iFixit calls a linear resonant actuator (LRA): a voice coil in a moving-mass assembly, 5.5 g, one in each Joy-Con (steps 17, 19 and 21)
Pair of powerful magnets flanking the voice coil in the HD Rumble actuator iFixit opened (step 21)
Lithium-ion battery, 1.9 Wh, in each Joy-Con (step 17)
IR camera with four IR LEDs in the red Joy-Con (step 19)
Macronix MX25U4033E 4 Mb CMOS flash on the red Joy-Con board (step 20)
